title: Changing Restaurant Ownership? Check Delivery Orders Before the First Shift
summary: Taking over an existing restaurant? Confirm each delivery app has transferred the storefront, verify order routing, and check the first payout separately.
body_markdown:
When you buy a restaurant, use each delivery platform’s ownership-transfer process for the existing storefront.


Verify that the buyer can manage it with their own account, that orders reach the kitchen, and that the correct business is set up to receive payouts. Match the first deposit separately. Don’t treat a still-visible listing as proof the transfer is complete.


## Identify the listing and the parties transferring it


For each marketplace, record the existing store ID and address, the authorized outgoing and incoming contacts, and the proposed transfer date. Keep one row per store and marketplace so an approval for one location is not mistaken for approval of the whole group. Don’t share passwords as a shortcut. Have the seller retain the historical records they are entitled to keep before access changes.


- DoorDash:


Its U.S.[change-of-ownership guide](https://help.doordash.com/en-us/merchants/article/change-of-ownership) describes a handover of the existing store. In a buyer-started transfer the previous owner must approve. Confirm the listed banking and order-routing steps for your case before treating the store as ready.
- Uber Eats:


Its[ownership-transfer guide](https://help.uber.com/merchants-and-restaurants/article/change-of-ownership?nodeId=29c12908-eb69-4bc0-8963-c8016c290f12) describes a single-store self-serve process in the U.S. and Canada and a separate route for multi-location requests. Confirm completion with the platform instead of using the requested date as proof.


If the store is changing address or brand too, ask the marketplace whether the same route applies before creating a second listing. Don’t assume ratings, settings or historical reports carry over the same way everywhere.


## Verify buyer access before the first delivery shift


Have the incoming manager sign in with their own approved access and confirm they can find the right store and see the expected menu, hours and status. Check the customer-facing address and listing. Then verify the kitchen receives an order through an approved test option, or observe the first legitimate order through acceptance and kitchen receipt if no approved test is available.


For example, the storefront may still look the same when the buyer uses a different point-of-sale (POS) system. If the marketplace says the transfer is complete but the new receiver has not been verified, record those two statuses separately. Confirm routing with the responsible provider before treating that channel as ready for normal volume.


## Check the first payout separately


Have finance verify the receiving business through the platform’s approved workflow. When the first payout is due, match the platform statement to the bank deposit. Identify any earlier adjustments separately and follow the platform guidance and transfer agreement rather than assuming a new login transferred responsibility for them.


Keep four statuses per storefront: transfer confirmed, buyer access verified, order receipt verified, first deposit matched


. Record who owns each exception and when they will check it again. A channel can be ready to take orders while its first settlement is still unverified.


Should a buyer create a new delivery listing for the same restaurant?


Start with the platform’s documented transfer process for the existing storefront. If the platform says a new listing is needed, follow that documented route instead of opening a duplicate on assumption.


For online and offline visibility across connected stores, explore[Voosh Marketplace Store Uptime](https://www.voosh.ai/marketplace-store-uptime) . Marketplace ownership, order receipt and payout verification remain separate checks.
